patient_information: A 34-year-old Malawian woman who was diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis 5 months prior to presentation. At that time, she was also found to be HIV-reactive with a baseline CD4 count of 54/μL. She is on antituberculous therapy, vitamin B6, antiretroviral therapy (ART), and co-trimoxazole prophylaxis.
chief_complaint: Slowly progressive weakness of the left arm and leg for approximately 3 months.
history_of_present_illness: The patient's problems began insidiously about 3 months earlier, starting with a limp in her left leg. The weakness progressed, and over the following weeks, her left arm also became affected. She has experienced slow, continuous progression since onset. She denies any head trauma, headache, recent fever, nausea, visual impairment, or weight loss. A review of systems was unremarkable.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is from Malawi and lives in an urban high-density area. She works as a street vendor selling mobile phone vouchers.
vitals: She is afebrile and her vital signs are normal.
physical_exam: General examination was normal apart from slightly pale conjunctivae. Fundoscopy was normal with no signs of papilledema or retinitis. The neurological examination revealed a spastic hemiparesis on the left with hyperreflexia. Power was graded 2/5 in the left leg and 3/5 in the left arm. A pronator drift was present on the left. Sensation of pain was reduced in her left leg and hand. Cranial nerve examination was normal.
labs_and_diagnostics: Full blood count showed WBC 3.8 x 10^9/L, hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, and platelets 140 x 10^9/L. Routine CSF examination was normal, and India Ink stain and fungal cultures were negative. A cerebral MRI scan showed multifocal T2 hyperintense lesions exclusively affecting the white matter, more prominent in the right hemisphere (frontal and temporal lobes), with a small area of demyelination in the left cerebellar peduncle.
differential_diagnosis: The primary differential was for focal brain lesions in an HIV-infected individual. Ischemic or hemorrhagic strokes were considered unlikely due to the subacute, progressive onset. Key considerations included cerebral toxoplasmosis, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), CNS lymphoma, cryptococcoma, and CNS tuberculosis (tuberculoma). The timing of onset, 2 months after starting ART, raised suspicion for Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS), which could unmask or paradoxically worsen a pre-existing CNS infection like PML or tuberculoma.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was started on empirical antitoxoplasmosis treatment with high-dose co-trimoxazole while continuing her ART and antituberculous therapy. Prednisolone 1mg/kg was added to cover for presumed IRIS. Her clinical status was unchanged at 4 weeks, and by 8 weeks, she showed further deterioration of power in her left hand. After the MRI findings, a presumed diagnosis of PML was made. She was referred to a rehabilitation centre for walking aids, and the palliative care team was involved.
final_diagnosis: A presumed diagnosis of Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML) was made, likely as a form of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (PML-IRIS). The diagnosis was based on the clinical picture of an insidious, progressive neurological deficit in a severely immunocompromised HIV patient who recently started ART. The diagnosis was supported by characteristic MRI findings of multifocal, non-enhancing T2 hyperintense lesions in the white matter and a lack of clinical response to empirical treatment for cerebral toxoplasmosis. PML is caused by the reactivation of the JC polyomavirus.
